mercy_translation.text:
The Word saw that human corruption could not otherwise be undone except through death. Yet it was impossible for the Word to die, since he is immortal and the Son of the Father. For this reason he takes to himself a body capable of dying, so that, because it had participated in the Word who is above all, it might be sufficient for death on behalf of all; and because of the Word who dwelt in it, it might remain incorruptible, and thereafter corruption might cease from all through the grace of the resurrection. Therefore, by offering to death the body he had taken to himself, like a sacred victim and sacrifice free from every stain, he immediately abolished death from all his fellow human beings by the offering of the appropriate body.

For because the Word of God is above all, by offering his own temple and bodily instrument as a life in exchange for all, he fulfilled what was owed in death. And thus, being united with all through the body like theirs, the incorruptible Son of God fittingly clothed all with incorruption in the promise concerning the resurrection. The very corruption in death no longer has a place against human beings because of the Word who dwelt among them through the one body.

It is as when a great king enters a large city and takes up residence in one of its houses: that entire city is considered worthy of great honor, and no enemy or robber any longer attacks and destroys it; rather, it receives every care because of the king who has taken up residence in one of its houses. So too has it happened with the King of all.

For when he came into our realm and dwelt in a body like ours, every hostile plot against human beings came to an end, and the corruption of death that had formerly held power over them vanished. The human race would have perished had not the Lord and Savior of all, the Son of God, come to bring death to an end.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The sacrificial vocabulary ἱερεῖον and θῦμα is rendered 'sacred victim and sacrifice.'
The analogy of the king dwelling in one house illustrates Athanasius' claim that the Word's embodiment benefits the whole human race.
